title: Rays make a worthwhile gamble in acquiring Freddy Peralta from Mets: MLB Trade Grades
author: Andy McCullough
content:
Mets get: OF Aidan Smith, INF Émilien Pitre, RHP Gary Gill Hill

Rays get: RHP Freddy Peralta

Mets: C
Rays: B

The return for Peralta was bound to disappoint. That’s inevitable when a player you acquired for two top-100 prospects — a deal we liked at the time! — looks like a shell of himself in his walk year. The return amounts to an exaggerated shoulder shrug: three guys who have a chance to help the Mets one day down the line, but none of them particularly inspiring. The highest-ranked prospect coming back is Aidan Smith, whom the Rays acquired from Seattle in the Randy Arozarena trade. Keith Law ranked Smith this spring as the Rays’ No. 19 prospect.

If there’s an organization you’d trust to turn “Fastball Freddy” into “Fastball Freddy” again, it’s the Rays. Get to work, Kyle Snyder and Rick Knapp. Fix Freddy Peralta and the Rays would have a formidable postseason top three: Peralta, Shane McClanahan and Drew Rasmussen. But that’s a big ask on a short timeline. There’s a reason Peralta wasn’t ranked alongside Tarik Skubal atop The Athletic’s trade deadline Big Board; no, he was well down the list, ranked 10th among starting pitchers, below the likes of Reid Detmers, Clay Holmes and Casey Mize.

If the Rays weren’t up for paying Skubal prices, Peralta is not a bad gamble as a low-risk, high-reward move. It’s a fine first step, anyway. Next, the Rays lineup needs real upgrades. — Stephen J. Nesbitt

Mets: B
Rays: B-

The Rays are still making the classics relevant, so when they acquire an underperforming arm, you’re not wrong to be suspicious. What do they know? What one weird trick are they going to teach Freddy Peralta? Are they going to move him six millimeters over on the rubber? Teach him the Vulcan change, or the ol’ dropsy-doo?

It’s possible that a trick won’t be necessary. Check out Peralta’s expected ERA (xERA) over the last few seasons:

2023: 3.35
2024: 3.83
2025: 3.43
2026: 3.82

He’s not that much different than he’s always been, then. The strikeout dip is both concerning and real, but there also isn’t a smoking gun in the underlying metrics, an alarming velocity dip or a breaking ball that just doesn’t have the same snap. Which is to say: The Rays are probably getting a solid pitcher, not a project. Bully for them.

The Mets get a couple of legitimate prospects, which speaks to the market for starting pitching at the deadline. As Law said when we asked him about the trade today, “Pitre is probably the guy the Mets wanted most — good player with great batted-ball data.”

Pitre is fascinating — a Québécois contact monster who can play all over the infield, but probably profiles best as a Luis Arraez-type second baseman and a fan-favorite in a best-case scenario. They’ll take a rock-solid utility player because those aren’t always easy to find, but they’re also free to dream big, and this would be a fun one.

I can already tell that I’m going to spend a few hours on this one if he’s any good. — Grant Brisbee

Mets: C+
Rays: B

If the Rays can fix Freddy Peralta’s delivery and help him regain the extension on his fastball, this trade might look like a coup. In the wake of Tarik Skubal coming off the board, it’s a gamble worth taking. The team has a deep farm system, so they may have given up real talent, but little that hampers their ability to make further moves.

The Mets must hope that this leg of the Peralta trade tree will go better than the first one. What a bummer of an outcome. The team dealt two of its legitimate prospects, Brandon Sproat and Jett Williams, to Milwaukee. The hope was that Peralta could headline a postseason rotation. Instead, he posted a 4.99 ERA, lost the life on his fastball and departed for a new team after four months.

Mets fans may note that neither Sproat nor Williams is setting the world ablaze in 2026 — perhaps that will give you pause before getting too excited about Smith, Pitre and Hill. The return is totally fine, especially given that Peralta has struggled this season and can become a free agent after the year. But it’s not how the Mets drew it up back in January, that’s for sure. — Andy McCullough
